key_features.classic_presentation: ONSET: SUDDEN, ACUTE onset within minutes to hours. Bimodal distribution: neonates and adolescents (12-18 years peak). May occur after trauma or during sleep. LOCATION: Affected testicle, may radiate to lower abdomen or groin. DURATION: CONSTANT pain since onset, progressively worsening. CHARACTER: SEVERE, SHARP, CONSTANT pain. AGGRAVATING: Movement, palpation of testicle. RELIEVING: NOTHING relieves pain. Lying still may decrease intensity slightly. TIMING: CONSTANT and unrelenting, worsens over time. Salvage rate <10% after 24 hours. SEVERITY: 9-10/10, SEVERE (patient often writhing in pain). ASSOCIATED SYMPTOMS: Nausea and vomiting (50%), high-riding testicle, horizontal lie of testicle, absent cremasteric reflex, scrotal swelling and erythema. NO relief with testicular elevation (negative Prehn's sign). KEY POSITIVES: Sudden severe testicular pain, adolescent male, nausea, high-riding testicle, absent cremasteric reflex. KEY NEGATIVES: Gradual onset over days suggests epididymitis. Relief with elevation suggests epididymitis.

red_flags: Any testicular pain >6 hours - irreversible ischemia developing, IMMEDIATE ER
Sudden severe testicular pain - ALWAYS emergent until proven otherwise
Absent cremasteric reflex with testicular pain - high suspicion for torsion
Nausea/vomiting with testicular pain - torsion until proven otherwise
